entries.shortDefinition: Thrust vector control steers a rocket or spacecraft by changing the direction in which its propulsion system produces force.
entries.fullDefinition: Methods include gimballing an engine or nozzle, moving part of a solid-rocket nozzle, injecting fluid into the exhaust, using vanes, or applying differential thrust among multiple engines. A guidance computer commands the system based on measured attitude, trajectory, and rates. TVC must respond quickly while carrying large loads and operating in vibration, heat, and pressure.
entries.whyItMatters: A launch vehicle needs control authority to maintain the commanded trajectory, counter winds and disturbances, manage engine-out conditions when designed for them, and orient itself for staging or insertion. TVC performance influences structural loads, navigation accuracy, stability, and payload environment.
entries.industryExample: On SLS, actuators move the RS-25 engines and booster nozzles to direct thrust and steer the vehicle during ascent. The relative contribution changes as boosters separate and the flight environment evolves.
entries.dontConfuse: TVC changes the direction of thrust; throttling changes its magnitude. A propulsion system may have one capability, both, or neither.
entries.evidenceNote: Directly supported by NASA technical references on SLS and solid- rocket thrust-vector control.

entries.shortDefinition: Thrust-to-weight ratio compares the force produced by a propulsion system with the weight of the vehicle or engine it must accelerate.
entries.fullDefinition: For a vehicle, TWR is commonly expressed as total thrust divided by weight under a stated gravity condition. A launch vehicle must have a liftoff TWR greater than one to rise from the pad, but the ratio changes as propellant is consumed, engines throttle, boosters separate, and local gravity varies. Engineers may also quote engine thrust-to-weight ratio, which compares an engine's thrust with the engine's own weight rather than the whole vehicle.
entries.whyItMatters: TWR influences initial acceleration, gravity losses, structural loads, crew comfort, engine-out margins, and trajectory design. A very low ratio can waste propellant fighting gravity; a very high ratio can create excessive loads or require throttling. The useful value therefore depends on mission phase and vehicle architecture.
entries.industryExample: A rocket may lift off with modest acceleration, then accelerate more strongly as its propellant mass decreases even if engine thrust remains nearly constant.
entries.dontConfuse: Always identify what weight is being used: the engine, a stage, or the complete vehicle. The number is meaningless without that scope and flight condition.
entries.evidenceNote: Grounded in NASA's thrust and rocket-equation references; the ratio follows directly from force and weight definitions.

entries.whyItMatters: It matters because it affects efficiency, thrust, complexity, temperature, pressure, reliability, and manufacturing. Misunderstanding it can propagate into requirements, cost, schedule, licensing, or operational risk.
entries.industryExample: A working mission applies the concept when an engine program trades performance against cost, risk, and operability, using cited requirements and reviewed assumptions.
entries.dontConfuse: Do not treat Staged Combustion Cycle as interchangeable with Thrust-to-Weight Ratio. They may be connected, but they describe different layers, conditions, or decisions in the system.

entries.shortDefinition: Specific impulse is a standard measure of how efficiently a rocket propulsion system uses propellant.
entries.fullDefinition: Specific impulse is thrust divided by propellant weight-flow rate and is commonly expressed in seconds. It is also equal to effective exhaust velocity divided by standard gravity. A higher Isp means the engine can produce more total impulse—or more ideal delta-v—for a given propellant mass. Values may differ at sea level and in vacuum because ambient pressure affects nozzle performance. Specific impulse must be interpreted together with thrust, mass, power, and mission duration.
entries.whyItMatters: Isp is central to comparing propulsion options and sizing propellant budgets. High-thrust chemical systems are effective for launch and rapid maneuvers, while electric propulsion can achieve much higher specific impulse but generally much lower thrust, requiring long burn times.
entries.industryExample: An operator choosing between chemical and electric orbit raising may trade schedule against propellant efficiency: chemical propulsion reaches the target orbit faster, while electric propulsion can preserve more spacecraft mass for payload or longer life.
entries.dontConfuse: Specific impulse is not thrust and not burn duration. An engine with high Isp may produce very little force, and a low-Isp motor can still generate enormous thrust.

entries.shortDefinition: A spacecraft is a vehicle designed to operate in space. It may carry people, cargo, instruments, or another vehicle, and it may itself be the destination.
entries.fullDefinition: Spacecraft include satellites, crew capsules, probes, landers, rovers, cargo vehicles, tugs, and space stations. Most combine a bus or service module—providing power, communications, thermal control, computing, attitude control, structure, and sometimes propulsion—with a mission payload. After separation from the launch vehicle, the spacecraft normally assumes responsibility for navigation, health management, communications, and mission execution.
entries.whyItMatters: The spacecraft is the operating asset that produces mission value. Its mass, dimensions, interfaces, power, thermal limits, pointing, data handling, propulsion, reliability, and regulatory status drive launch selection, testing, ground operations, insurance, and lifecycle cost.
entries.industryExample: A remote-sensing spacecraft carries an imaging payload while its bus supplies power, pointing, communications, data storage, and orbit control. A crew vehicle performs the same support functions while also sustaining and protecting people.
entries.dontConfuse: A spacecraft is not necessarily a satellite. Landers and suborbital vehicles are spacecraft but may not remain in orbit. The launch vehicle transports the spacecraft to its operational trajectory.
entries.evidenceNote: NASA and ESA directly define spacecraft and describe their major support and payload elements.

entries.shortDefinition: A satellite is an object that orbits another body. In the space industry, the word usually means an artificial spacecraft placed in orbit.
entries.fullDefinition: Natural satellites include moons; artificial satellites are engineered vehicles operating around Earth, another planet, the Moon, the Sun, or another body. A working satellite typically combines a spacecraft bus with one or more payloads. It can be active, inactive, operational, experimental, crewed, or uncrewed. A spacecraft traveling through space is not necessarily a satellite of a particular body until it is in orbit around that body.
entries.whyItMatters: Satellites provide communications, navigation, weather, Earth observation, science, timing, surveillance, and technology demonstration services. Their orbit, payload, ground segment, spectrum, licensing, reliability, and replacement strategy determine the service they can deliver.
entries.industryExample: An Earth-observation satellite uses its imaging payload to collect data while the bus controls attitude, stores data, communicates with ground stations, and maintains the orbit.
entries.dontConfuse: Every artificial satellite is a spacecraft, but not every spacecraft is a satellite. A lander, launch vehicle, or suborbital capsule may operate in space without orbiting.
entries.evidenceNote: NASA directly defines natural and artificial satellites and their relationship to orbit and spacecraft.

entries.shortDefinition: A satellite constellation is a group of satellites designed and operated as one coordinated system to deliver a shared mission or service.
entries.fullDefinition: Constellation design specifies the number of spacecraft, orbital planes, altitude, inclination, phasing, spacing, coverage, revisit, capacity, and replenishment strategy. Satellites may be similar or functionally complementary. The system also requires fleet-level command and control, ground-network access, inter-satellite or user links where applicable, collision-risk management, spectrum coordination, and deployment planning.
entries.whyItMatters: A constellation can provide global or persistent coverage that one satellite cannot, increase revisit frequency, distribute capacity, and create redundancy. It also multiplies manufacturing, launch, licensing, operations, cybersecurity, debris, and replacement challenges. The constellation—not the individual satellite—often becomes the commercial product architecture.
entries.industryExample: Navigation constellations use multiple orbital planes so users can see enough satellites for positioning. NASA’s A- Train coordinates several Earth-observing spacecraft so observations from different instruments can be combined.
entries.dontConfuse: A constellation is not the same as close formation flying. Constellation members may be widely separated; formation-flying spacecraft usually maintain tighter relative geometry and coordination.
entries.evidenceNote: NASA provides strong technical definitions and examples, though constellation architectures vary widely by mission.

entries.shortDefinition: A spacecraft bus is the platform that supports a mission payload by providing the essential services needed to survive and operate in space.
entries.fullDefinition: The bus usually includes structure, electrical power, command and data handling, communications, thermal control, attitude determination and control, navigation, propulsion, flight software, and interfaces to the launch vehicle and payload. A bus may be standardized across many missions or custom- designed for a single spacecraft. Its capabilities are defined by mass, power, pointing, data, thermal, propulsion, lifetime, and environmental limits.
entries.whyItMatters: Selecting a bus determines how quickly a mission can be developed and whether the payload's needs can be met. A proven platform can reduce nonrecurring engineering and integration risk, while a custom bus can optimize performance. Bus suppliers are therefore central nodes in the spacecraft supply chain.
entries.industryExample: The James Webb Space Telescope's bus provides power, communications, pointing, data handling, propulsion, and thermal support to the observatory. A commercial imaging satellite uses the same basic service categories at a much smaller scale.
entries.dontConfuse: The bus is not the payload. The bus keeps the spacecraft functioning; the payload performs the mission-specific sensing, communication, science, or service.
entries.evidenceNote: Directly supported by NASA's Webb spacecraft-bus description and 2026 spacecraft-platform survey.

entries.shortDefinition: A payload is the mission-specific equipment, instrument, cargo, or spacecraft capability carried by a launch vehicle or supported by a spacecraft bus.
entries.fullDefinition: Meaning depends on context. For a launch provider, the payload may be an entire satellite, crew vehicle, or cargo element delivered by the rocket. Within a spacecraft, the payload is usually the equipment that performs the primary mission, such as a camera, radar, communications repeater, telescope, scientific instrument, or hosted experiment. Payload requirements include mass, volume, power, data rate, pointing, thermal conditions, contamination, interfaces, and operational duty cycle.
entries.whyItMatters: The payload is usually the reason the mission exists, while its requirements drive the spacecraft bus, orbit, launch service, ground system, licensing, data architecture, and budget. Ambiguous use of the word can create serious interface errors between launch and spacecraft teams.
entries.industryExample: For an Earth-observation satellite, the imaging instrument is the spacecraft payload. From the rocket's perspective, however, the complete satellite is the launch payload.
entries.dontConfuse: Payload does not always mean paying cargo, and it does not have one universal system boundary. State the perspective being used.

entries.shortDefinition: Satellite Platform is a standardized or configurable spacecraft architecture used as the foundation for one or more mission payloads. It gives practitioners a common way to describe the product architecture that carries mission functions.
entries.fullDefinition: Engineering use requires more than the label: teams specify the applicable parameters, reference conditions, time interval, interfaces, and evidence. entries.whyItMatters: The concept shapes mass, interfaces, procurement, schedule, launch compatibility, and service life. It often becomes a decision point connecting engineers, operators, customers, suppliers, and regulators.
entries.industryExample: For example, a mission selects or customizes a platform around payload and orbit needs and records the result in the mission baseline.
entries.dontConfuse: Do not treat Satellite Platform as interchangeable with Payload. They may be connected, but they describe different layers, conditions, or decisions in the system.

entries.shortDefinition: A CubeSat is a small satellite built around a standardized modular form factor based on units called U.
entries.fullDefinition: The original 1U form factor is approximately a 10- centimeter cube, while larger configurations combine units into 2U, 3U, 6U, 12U, and other standardized arrangements. The CubeSat Design Specification defines mechanical and interface constraints that allow spacecraft to fit standardized dispensers. A CubeSat is still a complete spacecraft and may include power, communications, attitude control, propulsion, flight software, and one or more payloads.
entries.whyItMatters: Standardization lowers some integration barriers and lets universities, governments, and companies use common deployers, components, test practices, and launch opportunities. It does not eliminate mission engineering: power, thermal balance, radiation, communications, reliability, licensing, and debris mitigation remain real constraints.
entries.industryExample: A 6U CubeSat may carry a compact Earth-observation instrument and deploy from a rideshare dispenser after the primary payload has separated.
entries.dontConfuse: CubeSat describes a standardized form factor, not a guaranteed cost, quality level, mission type, or capability. Not every small satellite is a CubeSat.
entries.evidenceNote: Directly supported by NASA's CubeSat 101 resources and the NASA-hosted CubeSat Design Specification.

entries.canonicalName: Attitude Determination and Control System ADCS
entries.shortDefinition: ADCS is the spacecraft system that determines which way the vehicle is pointing and controls its orientation.
entries.fullDefinition: Attitude determination uses sensors such as star trackers, Sun sensors, Earth sensors, magnetometers, and gyroscopes to estimate orientation and rotation. Attitude control uses actuators such as reaction wheels, control-moment gyros, magnetic torquers, or thrusters to rotate or stabilize the spacecraft. Flight software combines sensor data, applies control laws, manages modes, and protects the spacecraft when measurements or actuators are limited.
entries.whyItMatters: Pointing affects communications links, solar-power generation, thermal conditions, imaging quality, propulsion burns, docking, and scientific observations. A spacecraft can be in the correct orbit yet fail its mission if it cannot point accurately or maintain stability.
entries.industryExample: An imaging satellite rotates to aim its instrument at a target, holds a stable line of sight during collection, then turns its antenna toward a ground station. ADCS coordinates the sensing, estimation, and actuation behind those maneuvers.
entries.dontConfuse: Attitude is orientation; orbit is the path around a body. ADCS controls where the spacecraft points, not necessarily where it travels.
entries.evidenceNote: Directly supported by NASA's 2026 guidance, navigation, and control survey and spacecraft-bus references.

entries.shortDefinition: Bandwidth is the span of frequencies occupied or available for a signal or channel. The term creates a shared reference for decisions involving a measure in the end-to-end communications chain.
entries.fullDefinition: Engineering use requires more than the label: teams specify the applicable parameters, reference conditions, time interval, interfaces, and evidence. The same term can be implemented differently across missions, but the underlying distinction must remain explicit and traceable.
entries.whyItMatters: It matters because it affects throughput, margin, availability, terminal design, power, and customer experience. Misunderstanding it can propagate into requirements, cost, schedule, licensing, or operational risk.
entries.industryExample: A working mission applies the concept when engineers calculate the metric for worst-case geometry and weather, using cited requirements and reviewed assumptions.
entries.dontConfuse: Bandwidth is a frequency span; data rate is the amount of information transferred per unit time.
entries.evidenceNote: Review draft synthesized from the listed primary or official sources; technical copy review and source-level verification remain required before publication.

entries.whyItMatters: It matters because it affects weather independence, spectral information, resolution, illumination, and application fit. Misunderstanding it can propagate into requirements, cost, schedule, licensing, or operational risk.
entries.industryExample: A working mission applies the concept when an EO provider selects a sensing mode to match the customer decision, using cited requirements and reviewed assumptions.
entries.dontConfuse: Do not treat Multispectral Imaging as interchangeable with Electro-Optical Imaging. They may be connected, but they describe different layers, conditions, or decisions in the system.

Its exact implementation can vary by mission, jurisdiction, standard, or provider, so professional use should state the applicable scope and version.
entries.whyItMatters: It matters because it affects heating, loads, guidance, landing, crew survival, and recovery. Misunderstanding it can propagate into requirements, cost, schedule, licensing, or operational risk.
entries.industryExample: A working mission applies the concept when a return vehicle follows a certified entry corridor and thermal design, using cited requirements and reviewed assumptions.
entries.dontConfuse: Do not treat Reentry Capsule as interchangeable with Thermal Protection System (TPS). They may be connected, but they describe different layers, conditions, or decisions in the system.

entries.shortDefinition: Acceptance Testing is testing performed on delivered flight or production hardware to confirm workmanship and compliance without intentionally consuming qualification margin. In industry use, it links technical meaning to a test or compatibility discipline used to demonstrate performance.
entries.fullDefinition: Engineering use requires more than the label: teams specify the applicable parameters, reference conditions, time interval, interfaces, and evidence. The same term can be implemented differently across missions, but the underlying distinction must remain explicit and traceable.
entries.whyItMatters: Its practical value appears in qualification margin, workmanship, mission environments, certification, and acceptance. Clear use of the term reduces interface errors and makes tradeoffs easier to audit.
entries.industryExample: For example, hardware is tested against a controlled plan before delivery or launch and records the result in the mission baseline.
entries.dontConfuse: Acceptance testing checks the delivered unit; qualification testing demonstrates design margin.
